aspects.says: With the default AbortPolicy, a task that finds the pool and the queue full is refused with RejectedExecutionException.
Since Java 19 an ExecutorService is AutoCloseable, and close() shuts it down and waits for its tasks.
A production pool is built directly with a bounded queue and a rejection policy, instead of the unbounded queue of newFixedThreadPool.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: newCachedThreadPool() has no bound on its threads, so sustained load can create thousands of them and exhaust memory.
CallerRunsPolicy runs a refused task on the submitting thread, which slows the producer and so gives backpressure.
aspects.reason: the pool practice builds the page's AbortPolicy pool and tests its refusal; the backpressure CallerRunsPolicy gives is a throughput effect on the producer that no deterministic test measures

aspects.says: An exception from a task run with execute() goes to the thread's uncaught-exception handler, while one from submit() is kept in the Future.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: Executor has only execute(Runnable); ExecutorService adds submit, invokeAll and shutdown; ScheduledExecutorService adds scheduling.
aspects.reason: a map of interface names; every practice on this page works through ExecutorService and ThreadPoolExecutor

aspects.says: A thread interrupted during awaitTermination() falls back to shutdownNow() and re-interrupts itself.
Submitting a null task throws NullPointerException.
aspects.reason: a one-line runtime rule with nothing further to practise

aspects.says: ThreadPoolExecutor's afterExecute() and terminated() hooks let a subclass monitor every task and the pool's end.
getActiveCount(), getCompletedTaskCount() and getQueue().size() let you observe a running pool.
aspects.reason: a list of getters; the pool practice's tests read getPoolSize() and getQueue() to check the submission flow

aspects.says: CPU-bound work gets about one thread per processor, and I/O-bound work a larger pool or virtual threads.
aspects.reason: a performance guideline that no deterministic test can observe; the fanout practice checks the observable part, one virtual thread per task

aspects.says: A task submitted after shutdown() is refused with RejectedExecutionException.
aspects.reason: the executor enforces it by itself, so no practice can get it wrong; the shutdown practice covers what shutdown does to tasks already submitted

aspects.says: newScheduledThreadPool() runs tasks after a delay or periodically.
aspects.reason: the page gives it one table row and no example; a delayed or periodic run depends on the wall clock, which the practices keep out of their tests

aspects.says: shutdown() stops new work but finishes running and queued tasks; shutdownNow() interrupts running tasks and returns the ones never started.
newSingleThreadExecutor() runs its tasks one at a time, in submission order, on one thread.
StructuredTaskScope, a Java 21 preview, manages a group of related tasks as a unit.
aspects.reason: a preview API that needs --enable-preview, which the practices' Java 21 build does not turn on; the page only names it

aspects.says: A ThreadPoolExecutor starts core threads first, then queues, and starts threads beyond the core size only once the queue is full.
A custom ThreadFactory names the pool's threads and can make them daemons, so thread dumps are readable.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: The two-phase idiom calls shutdown() and awaitTermination(), and falls back to shutdownNow() when the wait times out.
newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() gives every task its own virtual thread, so there is no pool size to limit how many run at once.
Virtual threads let far more I/O-bound tasks wait at once, but they do not make any single task faster.
